There's an old joke that Apple solemnly declares every year's iPhone Pro to be "the best iPhone we've ever made," as if that were some huge revelation. But I do genuinely feel a certain poignancy about the iPhone 18 Pro, because if the rumours about next year's model are accurate, this phone may well be the final iteration of the design language that began with the 2017 iPhone X.

Specifically, we expect to see the next major step towards the "single slab of glass" vision next year, bringing an end to this decade of incremental change…

The iPhone Pro Evolution

If you place the iPhone 12 Pro through to the iPhone 16 Pro side by side, I think most people would struggle to tell them apart on looks alone, apart from the 2022 switch from notch to Dynamic Island. The iPhone 17 Pro was the exception, thanks to the extended camera plateau and Cosmic Orange colourway.

Of course, each generation brings new features, but I'd argue that, unless a particular model has special significance for you personally, skipping two or three generations barely delivers a noticeable improvement in the user experience.

This is absolutely no criticism of Apple. The fact is that the high-end smartphone is a mature technology, at least in terms of its conventional form factor. You simply can't achieve huge differences between adjacent generations when there's only so much you can improve in an annual update cycle.

Apple is now starting to experiment with different form factors, beginning with the iPhone Air, and now of course the iPhone Duo—and we also expect another major design breakthrough next year, with a special model to mark the 20th anniversary.

Exactly how Apple will position next year's new design remains unclear. Some initially thought it would be a standalone model outside the iPhone 19 Pro range, but other reports suggest it will be next year's Pro model. There's also the question of whether Apple will use consecutive numbering or skip a number to mark the milestone, so it might even be called the iPhone 20 Pro.

Personally, I do expect it to be the new iPhone Pro design, whether Apple calls it 19 or 20. If so, that makes the iPhone 18 Pro the final version of this design language we've had for six years.

I'm skipping two generations from the iPhone 16 Pro, so I'll list separately what each year's model brings me. I'll skip some that I consider unimportant or entirely irrelevant to me, like going from a 6-core GPU to a 7-core GPU and GenLock.

iPhone 17 Pro brought…

  • Center Stage front camera for photos and video calls
  • Ultra-stable video recording
  • Dual-camera simultaneous recording
  • Telephoto zoom increased from 5x to 8x
  • Telephoto sensor increased from 12MP to 48MP
  • ProRes RAW video recording
  • Better battery life
  • Faster charging speeds

iPhone 18 Pro brings…

  • Larger maximum aperture for main camera
  • Variable aperture for main camera
  • Pro camera controls (aperture, shutter speed, white balance, histogram)
  • Photographic Styles 3rd generation
  • Intelligent focus tracking
  • Cinematic mode effects added to standard video
  • Tap-to-zoom and rotate added to front camera
  • Smaller Dynamic Island, with three simultaneous Live Activities
  • (Even) better battery life
  • (Even) faster charging speeds

My personal… highlights

Personally, there are five features I'll be watching for during my early use.

Variable aperture lens

Although the most headline-grabbing feature is the variable aperture lens, I've said before that expectations shouldn't be set too high. On a sensor this small, the maximum aperture is only marginally larger, so I don't expect to see a huge difference in terms of shallow depth of field.

However, the larger maximum aperture does let in a bit more light—around two-thirds of a stop. How much difference that makes in practice remains to be seen, but in theory it should shorten Night mode exposure times. Night mode is a feature I use a lot, and mostly handheld, so I'm very much looking forward to trying it out.

Pro camera controls

Being able to manually control shutter speed will definitely be useful for things like pan shots. Having full control over white balance will definitely be useful too. And I expect the histogram will help when manually setting exposure.

For taking photos or editing them on the iPhone, I'm generally not a big fan of filters, preferring to edit afterwards using traditional adjustments. So I rarely use the existing Photographic Styles feature and don't expect to use its latest version much more. But I have to say the Film preset there does intrigue me, so I'll definitely give it a try.

One of the biggest weaknesses of autofocus when shooting video is that, when the subject is briefly occluded by other objects, the camera may shift focus to those obstructions. Intelligent focus tracking claims to address this problem, so I'll definitely be testing it in practice.

Cinematic mode effects added to standard video

I said barely two months ago that Apple seemed to have forgotten about Cinematic mode video. I said it was a pity, because if Cinematic mode video were done well, it would absolutely be a game-changer for turning the iPhone into a more serious video-making device. It's always been just that bit short of perfect, which is frustrating.

But it seems I was wrong: one of the iPhone 18's new features is the ability to apply Cinematic-style video effects to video shot in standard mode.

No longer having to decide whether to use the mode before shooting is certainly convenient, but what interests me most is that Apple is paying attention to this feature again. That's a sign it's getting real focus, so we have reason to expect it will continue to improve, like Portrait mode has done for stills. I'm really looking forward to trying this feature.

So those are the features I think may make the biggest impact on me. How about you? If you've already upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro, which features were the ones that made you switch? Feel free to share in the comments.
